scenes.visual: Title card 'Receptors First, Antigen Chooses' over a row of GREY lymphocytes, each with a differently notched receptor. COLOUR MAP (shared by both films, take-homes and text): V segments BLUE, D segments GREEN, J segments ORANGE; ordinary lymphocytes GREY circles; the selected clone GOLD; memory cells GOLD with a dark outline; antibody in plasma a PURPLE bar; antigen a small RED spiky shape. Every number appears only as on-screen text. No molecular structures: cells are circles, receptors are simple notched shapes, DNA is a row of labelled cards.

scenes.tts: Your body already holds cells that can bind viruses you have never met. How could it prepare for something it has never seen?
scenes.visual: A RED spiky virus labelled 'never met before' drifts toward a crowd of GREY cells; one cell's notched receptor already matches its shape, and a question mark hangs over the pair.
scenes.narration: Your body already holds cells that can bind viruses you have never met. How could it prepare for something it has never seen?

scenes.tts: There are two possible answers. A soft, general receptor might fold itself around each new antigen, like clay. Or receptors could be made first, and the antigen picks one that fits.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left, labelled 'instructive idea': a blob of grey clay presses itself around the RED antigen. Right, labelled 'selection': a shelf of ready-made notched keys; the RED antigen slides along and stops at the one that fits.
scenes.narration: There are two possible answers. A soft, general receptor might fold itself around each new antigen, like clay. Or receptors could be made first, and the antigen picks one that fits.

scenes.tts: Adaptive immunity is carried by lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell. The molecule a lymphocyte's receptor binds is called an antigen.
scenes.visual: Labels appear: 'lymphocyte (B cell or T cell)' points to a GREY circle; 'receptor' points to its notched tip; 'antigen' points to the RED shape.
scenes.narration: Adaptive immunity is carried by lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell. The molecule a lymphocyte's receptor binds is called an antigen.

scenes.tts: Macfarlane Burnet proposed the second answer, called clonal selection. Nearly every lymphocyte makes receptors of one shape. It makes them before it meets the antigen they fit.
scenes.visual: Caption 'Macfarlane Burnet, 1957: clonal selection'. The left clay panel fades out. The shelf of keys becomes a row of GREY lymphocytes, each with one notch shape, labelled 'nearly every cell: one receptor shape, made before antigen'.
scenes.narration: Macfarlane Burnet proposed the second answer, called clonal selection. Nearly every lymphocyte makes receptors of one shape. It makes them before it meets the antigen they fit.

scenes.tts: But the human genome holds far fewer protein-coding genes than there are receptor shapes. So how can it make millions of them?
scenes.visual: A box labelled 'genome: about 20,000 protein-coding genes' sits beside a much larger cloud of receptor shapes labelled 'millions of receptors'; an arrow between them carries a question mark.
scenes.narration: But the human genome holds far fewer protein-coding genes than there are receptor shapes. So how can it make millions of them?

scenes.tts: For a worked example, follow one developing B cell as it builds the heavy chain of its antibody. The tip of that chain is not encoded as one piece. It is built from short stretches of DNA, called gene segments. Here they sit in three rows: V segments, D segments and J segments.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one GREY cell labelled 'developing B cell' to a strip of DNA labelled 'antibody heavy-chain genes', drawn as cards in three rows: a long row of BLUE cards labelled 'V', a row of GREEN cards labelled 'D', a short row of ORANGE cards labelled 'J'. Small counters beside each row: 'V: 40', 'D: 23', 'J: 6' (illustrative human counts).
scenes.narration: For a worked example, follow one developing B cell as it builds the heavy chain of its antibody. The tip of that chain is not encoded as one piece. It is built from short stretches of DNA, called gene segments. Here they sit in three rows: V segments, D segments and J segments.

scenes.tts: The cell picks one V, one D and one J. Enzymes cut the DNA, and the cell joins the three chosen pieces. That joined piece encodes the tip of one heavy chain.
scenes.visual: One BLUE, one GREEN and one ORANGE card lift out of their rows; the cards between them slide away; the three snap together into a BLUE-GREEN-ORANGE bar labelled 'heavy chain tip'. The bar becomes the notch on the cell's receptor.
scenes.narration: The cell picks one V, one D and one J. Enzymes cut the DNA, and the cell joins the three chosen pieces. That joined piece encodes the tip of one heavy chain.

scenes.tts: The screen shows illustrative human counts for each row. The cell takes one segment from each row. Do the choices add up, or multiply?
scenes.visual: The three rows again with counters '40', '23', '6'. Two answer cards appear: 'add: 40 + 23 + 6 = ?' and 'multiply: 40 x 23 x 6 = ?'.
scenes.narration: The screen shows illustrative human counts for each row. The cell takes one segment from each row. Do the choices add up, or multiply?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The two answer cards hold; a 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: They multiply. Every V can go with every D, and every such pair with every J. So a few dozen segments give thousands of V-D-J combinations for the heavy chain's variable region.
scenes.caption: They multiply. Every V can go with every D, and every such pair with every J. So 69 segments give 5,520 V-D-J combinations for the heavy chain's variable region.
scenes.visual: The 'add' card shows '69' and dims. The 'multiply' card fills in: '40 x 23 = 920', then '920 x 6 = 5,520'. A fan of BLUE-GREEN-ORANGE bars spreads out behind it, too many to count, labelled '5,520 V-D-J combinations (heavy-chain variable region)'.
scenes.narration: They multiply. Every V can go with every D, and every such pair with every J. So 69 segments give 5,520 V-D-J combinations for the heavy chain's variable region.

scenes.tts: And that is only one chain. Light chains use just V and J segments. T cells build their own receptor chains from segments of their own. Imprecise joins and chain pairing multiply the variety further.
scenes.visual: Small icons slide in under the fan: 'light chain: V + J only', 'T cell receptors: their own segments', 'imprecise joins', 'pairing', the last two each with a 'x' sign; the fan grows into a dense cloud labelled 'millions of shapes, before any antigen'.
scenes.narration: And that is only one chain. Light chains use just V and J segments. T cells build their own receptor chains from segments of their own. Imprecise joins and chain pairing multiply the variety further.

scenes.tts: So the body holds a vast crowd of lymphocytes, each with its own receptor. It is like a shoe shop with millions of pairs already on the shelves, waiting for the right customer.
scenes.visual: Pull back to a wide crowd of GREY lymphocytes with varied notches. It morphs briefly into long shelves of shoes, each pair different, then back to the cells.
scenes.narration: So the body holds a vast crowd of lymphocytes, each with its own receptor. It is like a shoe shop with millions of pairs already on the shelves, waiting for the right customer.

scenes.tts: Now an antigen arrives. It drifts past B cell after B cell, and most receptors ignore it. It binds only the few whose receptors already fit. T cells need the antigen shown to them on another cell, as the text explains.
scenes.visual: A RED antigen floats along a crowd of GREY B cells, bouncing off mismatched notches. It docks on one cell whose notch matches; that cell turns GOLD. A small corner note: 'T cells: antigen must be displayed on another cell (see text)'.
scenes.narration: Now an antigen arrives. It drifts past B cell after B cell, and most receptors ignore it. It binds only the few whose receptors already fit. T cells need the antigen shown to them on another cell, as the text explains.

scenes.tts: Those cells divide. Their descendants form a clone, a population descended from one cell, all starting with the same receptor.
scenes.visual: The GOLD cell splits into two, then four, then a small GOLD cluster, every cell with the same notch, labelled 'clone'. The GREY cells around it stay unchanged.
scenes.narration: Those cells divide. Their descendants form a clone, a population descended from one cell, all starting with the same receptor.

scenes.tts: The antigen did not mold that receptor. It existed before the antigen arrived. The antigen chooses; it does not shape.
scenes.visual: Side by side: the GOLD notch just before the antigen arrived and at first contact, identical, with an equals sign, labelled 'first receptor: not molded by antigen'. The clay panel from the start reappears briefly and is crossed out.
scenes.narration: The antigen did not mold that receptor. It existed before the antigen arrived. The antigen chooses; it does not shape.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. LINE: 'Receptors come first; the antigen only chooses which cells multiply.'
